flashcards.q: What does a native <button> get for free that a <div role="button"> does not?
flashcards.a: Keyboard focusability, Enter AND Space both firing click, role reported to the accessibility tree, and form participation -- all automatically. A div needs manual tabindex="0", a keydown handler for both keys, the role attribute, and an accessible name.

flashcards.q: Why is "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA" literally true, not just a slogan?
flashcards.a: ARIA only changes what's reported to the accessibility tree -- it never changes actual browser behavior (focus, keyboard handling). An incorrect ARIA attribute actively tells an assistive technology user something false about the element, which is worse than an honest absence of any claim.

flashcards.q: List the four required focus-management behaviors for an accessible modal, in order.
flashcards.a: 1) Move focus into the modal on open. 2) Trap focus inside while open (Tab/Shift+Tab wrap at the boundaries). 3) Close on Escape. 4) Restore focus to the trigger element on close.

flashcards.q: Why can a form validation error be clearly visible on screen but completely silent to a screen reader?
flashcards.a: Content injected into the DOM with no aria-live ancestor and no focus movement to it produces no announcement -- screen readers announce content on navigation/focus or inside a configured live region, not on any DOM mutation.

polite waits for the user's current activity to finish before announcing (most updates). assertive interrupts immediately -- reserve for genuinely urgent content (session expiry, critical errors); overuse is disorienting.

flashcards.q: Why does client-side routing in an SPA break something multi-page sites got for free, and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: A full page load resets focus and announces the new title as a side effect; an SPA route change does neither automatically. Fix: move focus to the new page's <h1 tabIndex={-1}> and update document.title on route change.

flashcards.q: Why tabIndex={-1} rather than tabIndex={0} on a heading used for post-navigation focus?
flashcards.a: tabIndex={-1} makes it programmatically focusable via .focus() without adding it to the natural Tab order -- it should only be a one-time landing point right after navigation, not a normal Tab stop.

flashcards.q: What percentage of WCAG issues does automated testing (axe-core) catch on average, and what does that imply?
flashcards.a: Roughly 57% on average (real-world data across 13K+ pages). A passing automated scan is a necessary floor, not proof of accessibility -- manual keyboard-only and screen-reader testing is required for the rest.

flashcards.q: What are WCAG 2.2's three conformance levels and which one is the practical/legal target?
flashcards.a: A (floor, unusable-if-missing), AA (4.5:1 text contrast, visible focus, consistent nav -- referenced by ADA case law, Section 508, EN 301 549), AAA (7:1 contrast, highest bar). AA is the realistic target for virtually every product; W3C doesn't recommend AAA as a universal target.
Use a native HTML element or attribute instead of re-purposing an element and adding ARIA, whenever a native option with the needed semantics and behavior exists.

flashcards.q: What contrast ratios does WCAG AA require?
flashcards.a: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and UI components.

flashcards.q: Why prefer behavior-correct component libraries (Radix UI, React Aria, Headless UI) over hand-rolling complex widgets like combobox or tree?
flashcards.a: These patterns have many documented keyboard-interaction edge cases (per the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide) that are expensive to get right and easy to regress; a shared, battle-tested library solves it once instead of every team re-solving it independently.
